findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
findings.headline: Nine schemes carried forward from 2024/25 with zero 2025/26 expenditure; requesting carry-forward again into 2026/27
findings.detail: Annex C lists schemes including High Needs Block (£2.46m), Simpler Recycling (£1.78m), Basic Need Grant (£1.29m), LA Housing Fund (£0.40m) - all with 0% 2025/26 spend despite prior-year carry-forward. Council seeks Cabinet approval to carry these forward again, acknowledging they represent schemes 'where budget was carried forward from 2024/25'.
findings.matters: Multi-year non-spend suggests projects may not be delivery-ready; capital tied up without clear delivery route; pattern indicates project preparation or approvals issues
findings.figures: 9 schemes total: High Needs £2.46m, Simpler Recycling £1.78m, Basic Need Grant £1.29m, LA Housing £0.40m (all 0% spend)
findings.quote: The carry-forward analysis identifies schemes where carry-forward is requested despite no in-year outturn and where budget was carried forward from 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
findings.headline: Council redirected capital receipt to revenue support ('flexible use') due to 'significant pressure on revenue budget' from government funding settlement
findings.detail: Significant capital receipt from March 2026 asset disposal was not used to finance capital programme, but instead used to fund 'flexible use of capital receipts strategy' to address revenue pressures. This reflects structural pressure from '3-year funding settlement announced by Government from 2026/27'.
findings.matters: Revenue-side stress forcing capital receipts to be used for revenue support rather than capital financing; signals structural revenue deficit; reduces capital financing flexibility
findings.figures: Not quantified in report
findings.quote: This could have been used to help finance the capital programme but has been used instead to finance the Council's flexible use of capital receipts strategy, recognising the significant pressure on the revenue budget from the three-year funding settlement announced by the Government from 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £20.7m year-on-year to £239.6m; council 'gradually moving away from ability to internally fund capital investment'
findings.detail: CFR reached £239.6m as at 31 March 2026. Actual borrowing £127.5m with net debt £115.971m represents increase of £20.7m from 2024/25. Report explicitly states this reflects 'gradual movement away from the Council being able to internally fund its capital investment'.
findings.matters: Rapid rise in CFR signals deteriorating financial position and increasing reliance on borrowing; reduces financial headroom and increases exposure to interest rate risk; trend unsustainable if capital underdelivery persists
findings.figures: CFR £239.6m, borrowing £127.5m, net debt £115.971m, YoY increase £20.7m
findings.quote: This is an increase of £20.7m from 2024/25 and reflects the gradual movement away from the Council being able to internally fund its capital investment.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
findings.headline: Binfield Community Hub: main contractor entered administration; £180k supplementary capital approval needed for retention works
findings.detail: Construction completed in 2024/25 on budget, but outstanding retention and defect works (£179k) were not anticipated. Main contractor went into administration, forcing the council into prolonged negotiations with administrator. Supplementary capital approval requested for 2026/27 to complete work.
findings.matters: Contractor insolvency in major project delivery creates operational and financial risk; illustrates third-party delivery risk in capital programme; requires emergency capital allocation
findings.figures: £179,000 identified as works outstanding; supplementary capital approval requested
findings.quote: This has been complicated due to the fact that the main contractor went into administration and the council has been in prolonged discussions with the administrator regarding the outstanding work. These discussions are still ongoing however a value of £179,000 has been identified as works outstanding.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
findings.headline: Warfield Community Hub - £12.9m of £13.4m budget unspent; site start delayed by extended design period
findings.detail: Largest single carry-forward in the programme: £13.43m budget, only £0.53m (4%) spent in 2025/26, £12.90m (96%) carried forward. Delay caused by extended design and planning determination. This is the primary driver of Communities directorate underperformance.
findings.matters: Largest unspent scheme in the portfolio; delay in major asset delivery suggests design/planning risk and project management challenge; delivery confidence questionable given 96% carry-forward
findings.figures: £13.42m budget, £0.53m outturn (4%), £12.89m carry-forward (96%)
findings.quote: The largest carry-forward request relates to Warfield Community Hub, where the 2025/26 estimate was adjusted to reflect a delayed start on site arising from an extended design period and planning determination.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
findings.headline: Communities directorate delivered only 14% of £19m capital budget; 85% carry-forward
findings.detail: Communities budget of £19.02m resulted in outturn of £2.66m, with £16.21m (85%) carried forward. This is far weaker than Place (30% carry-forward) and People (62%), and is driven by Warfield Community Hub (£12.9m unspent), Simpler Recycling (£1.78m unspent), and Cemetery Extension (£0.59m unspent).
findings.matters: Directorate-level underperformance raises questions about project readiness and delivery management in a key service area; 85% carry-forward cannot be attributed to normal multi-year schemes
findings.figures: Communities: £19,021,050 budget, £2,661,017 outturn (14%), £16,214,809 carry-forward (85%)

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 46% of budgeted expenditure; 54% of £84.3m requested as carry-forward
findings.detail: Against profiled budget of £84.32m, the council spent £38.82m in 2025/26 and requests carry-forward of £45.33m into 2026/27. The council acknowledges this represents 'budgets profiled ahead of realistic scheme readiness' and commits to stronger gateway discipline and quarterly profiling from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.matters: Persistent underdelivery relative to budget signals execution risk; lenders assess capability to deploy capital efficiently and to service borrowing taken to finance schemes that take longer to complete
findings.figures: £38.82m outturn, £84.32m budget (46%), £45.33m carry-forward (54%)
findings.quote: The level of expenditure represents 46.0% of the profiled budget. Carry-forward into 2026/27 is requested for £45.32m, equivalent to 53.8% of the budget.

findings.headline: Transformation savings programmes failed to deliver £0.654m of planned savings
findings.detail: The Digitisation and Efficiency and the Neighbourhood Assets & Regeneration Business Change Programmes did not achieve £0.654m of budgeted savings. These programmes are typically relied upon to offset structural budget pressures in future years; slippage suggests the council may not have a clear path to balance in coming years.
findings.matters: If these programmes cannot deliver, the council will need to find alternative savings or accept larger deficits; this affects forecasting confidence for 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.figures: £0.654m of budgeted savings not achieved across two programmes.
findings.quote: Budgeted savings were not achieved for the Digitisation and Efficiency and the Neighbourhood Assets & Regeneration Business Change Programmes (£0.654m)

findings.headline: Structural income losses from government funding changes and Business Rates policy
findings.detail: Section 31 grant income fell by £0.318m due to the multiplier cap and relief changes. More broadly, the council faces ongoing financial pressures from the introduction of a new funding system and Business Rates reset by central government. These are structural changes, not one-off adjustments, requiring sustained mitigation.
findings.matters: Structural income reductions cannot be solved by spending controls alone; they force reliance on reserves or require service cuts, both of which constrain financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Section 31 grant reduction of £0.318m; broader funding system changes and Business Rates reset.
findings.quote: The Council continues to face ongoing financial pressures due to the introduction of a new funding system and Business Rates reset by Central Government and increases in demand led pressures.

findings.headline: Autumn 2025 overspend projection forced emergency spending controls mid-year
findings.detail: In Autumn 2025, the council was tracking to an overspend and responded with emergency controls: curtailing non-essential expenditure and reviewing all recruitment requests. These control measures proved necessary to prevent a year-end overspend, indicating the underlying budget position was weaker than anticipated and required significant mid-course correction.
findings.matters: A council that needs emergency spending freezes mid-year is running with insufficient budget resilience; this points to structural misalignment between budgeted and actual costs.
findings.figures: An overspend was projected in Autumn 2025; controls were introduced and proved effective.
findings.quote: In Autumn 2025 an overspend position was projected for the Council and the Corporate Management Team introduced several control measures, including curtailing non-essential expenditure and reviewing all recruitment requests, to ensure the budget was not overspent at the year end.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care placements overspent by £1.620m, requiring emergency draw on corporate contingency
findings.detail: Care and accommodation for children in care exceeded budget by £1.620m, driven by children's home placements (£0.810m), independent fostering (£0.333m), semi-independent living (£0.230m) and care leavers placements (£0.181m). This was only brought to zero variance by allocating £1.040m from the corporate contingency reserve. The overspend signals underlying demand-led pressures that budgets did not anticipate.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends in social care suggest the underlying cost drivers are not well understood or controllable; this pattern can recur in future years and erode contingency buffers.
findings.figures: £1.620m overspend; £1.040m from corporate contingency used to offset it.
findings.quote: care and accommodation costs for Children Looked After overspent (£1.620m) primarily from Children's Home Placements (£0.810m), Independent Fostering costs (£0.333m), Semi Independent Living costs (£0.230m) and the cost of Care Leavers placements (£0.181m). The overall variance was reduced to nil following a £1.040m allocation from the Corporate Contingency to support demand led budgets.

findings.headline: Schools Budget deficit has grown to over £32m with uncertain medium-term funding arrangements
findings.detail: The schools budget deficit increased to over £32m during 2025/26. The council has applied for a government grant under the SEND Reform Plan scheme to write off 90% of deficits accrued to end of 2025/26. However, arrangements for future costs between now and March 2028 remain unresolved, creating uncertainty about how the deficit will be managed during that critical window.
findings.matters: A £32m deficit is a massive contingent liability; if the government scheme is delayed or the interim arrangement terms are unfavorable, the council could face sudden pressure on cash and reserves.
findings.figures: Over £32m deficit; 90% of 2025/26 deficits will be written off by grant; future arrangements unclear.
findings.quote: the deficit on the Schools Budget has increased to over £32m during 2025/26...Future costs beyond 31 March 2028 will be funded by Central Government, with arrangements between now and then subject to further clarification.

findings.headline: Leisure services hit with £0.260m utility indemnification charges, including £0.019m backdated to prior year
findings.detail: Leisure reported a £0.243m overspend, almost entirely driven by utility indemnification charges totalling £0.260m. Of this, £0.019m relates to 2024/25, indicating the council was exposed to a prior-year liability that emerged in-year.
findings.matters: Backdated utility indemnification charges suggest either hidden contingent liabilities on leisure assets or exposure to supplier disputes. The size (£0.260m) and the fact it includes prior-year items suggests this may recur.
findings.figures: Leisure overspend: £0.243m. Utility Indemnification charges: £0.260m, of which £0.019m is 2024/25 backdated.
findings.quote: The overspend within Leisure relates to the Utility Indemnification charges applicable across the sites, this totals £0.260m and includes £0.241m relating to 25/26 plus an additional £0.019m relating to 24/25.

findings.headline: Education and Learning Fleet & Transport costs overspent by £0.737m with savings targets unmet
findings.detail: Fleet & Transport reported a £0.737m overspend, with additional pressure of £0.099m in SEND support services (legal and mediation costs). The council's managed vacancy savings across the service did not materialize, creating a further pressure of £0.297m. These pressures in a core People service are not one-off.
findings.matters: A major directorate (People) reporting unmet savings and growing transport costs signals either unrealistic budgeting or operational control issues in a core service.
findings.figures: Fleet & Transport: £0.737m overspend. SEND support services: £0.099m pressure. Unmet vacancy savings: £0.297m.
findings.quote: There was an overspend within Fleet & Transport of £0.737m which was partially offset by underspends within staffing (-£0.075m) to create an overall pressure of £0.662m. Alongside this was a further pressure (£0.099m) within SEND support services where legal and mediation costs were greater than originally anticipated. In addition, the savings represented within the managed vacancy factor across the service were not met resulting in a further pressure of £0.297m.

findings.headline: Cash resources are being depleted and the council is shifting to short-term borrowing
findings.detail: The treasury report explicitly states the council's cash resources are declining, exacerbated by the schools deficit. Net borrowing rose from £95.245m to £115.971m in one year. Long-term PWLB borrowing remained flat at £60m, but short-term market loans jumped from £45m to £67.5m, all maturing within 258 days. Internal borrowing (using reserves instead of borrowing) is no longer feasible.
findings.matters: Rising reliance on short-term borrowing signals the council can no longer use its reserves as a financial buffer. Interest rate risk is exposed across a large maturity wall of short-term loans.
findings.figures: Net borrowing: £95.245m (Mar 25) to £115.971m (Mar 26), a £20.7m increase. Short-term borrowing: £45m to £67.5m. CFR: £232m to £239.6m.
findings.quote: The Council's cash resources are gradually being depleted, exacerbated by the continuing rise in the dedicated schools grant deficit due to increasing costs of education for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities. As a consequence, actual net borrowing costs during 2025/26 were £0.056m more than anticipated.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care demand overspend of £1.62m required emergency contingency support
findings.detail: Children Looked After costs overspent by £1.620m in a single year, driven by Children's Home Placements (£0.810m), Independent Fostering (£0.333m), Semi-Independent Living (£0.230m), and Care Leavers placements (£0.181m). This overspend was covered only by a £1.040m allocation from Corporate Contingency, leaving no margin for further pressure.
findings.matters: This is a demand-led service where the council has no direct control. A £1.6m overspend in one year signals either forecasting failure or uncontrollable demographic pressures, and the council had to raid contingency to balance it.
findings.figures: £1.620m total care and accommodation overspend, including £0.810m Children's Homes, £0.333m fostering. £1.040m contingency allocation.
findings.quote: The significant care and accommodation costs for Children Looked After overspent by £1.620m primarily from Children's Home Placements (£0.810m), Independent Fostering costs (£0.333m), Semi Independent Living costs (£0.230m) and the cost of Care Leavers placements (£0.181m).

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £32.4m and Safety Valve support is ending
findings.detail: The schools budget deficit has grown from £9.3m in March 2022 to £32.4m in March 2026. The government's Safety Valve programme, which was funding 90% of the deficit, is being wound down. The council's own Safety Valve Reserve fell from £22.761m to £5.761m in a single year, indicating the council is now funding the 10% gap itself.
findings.matters: A growing, unfunded deficit in the schools block is a structural budget problem. As Safety Valve support ends, this becomes a direct call on the council's own resources with no solution mechanism in place.
findings.figures: DSG Adjustment Account: March 25 -£24.650m, March 26 -£32.405m. Safety Valve Reserve: March 25 £22.761m, March 26 £5.761m
findings.quote: The safety valve programme has now been disbanded as a separate Government initiative, and the government has committed to meeting 90% of the deficit accrued to the end of 2025/26.

findings.headline: Building Control is structurally insolvent and cannot be fixed
findings.detail: Building Control income has declined every year since 2016/17 and has never covered its costs. The 2025/26 variance shows £0.112m income shortfall and £0.142m agency staffing overspend. The paper states explicitly that "external, non-local authority competition makes it unlikely income will ever offset costs".
findings.matters: A service that operates at a permanent loss and cannot be fixed is a cost centre the council cannot shed; it signals either resignation to subsidy or inability to rationalize.
findings.figures: £0.112m income underachievement, £0.142m agency overspend, £0.230m net variance in 2025/26
findings.quote: Actual income has been in decline since 2016/17 and service has never achieved the necessary income level to offset deficits on account. External, non-local authority competition makes is unlikely income will ever offset costs.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Flexible use of capital receipts strategy becoming more aggressive due to difficult three-year funding position
findings.detail: The council has increased the ambition of its Flexible Use of Capital Receipts strategy (first adopted November 2023) to fund transformation and business change from capital receipts, a shift driven by explicitly stated 'particularly difficult funding position for the next three years'.
findings.matters: Reliance on one-off capital receipts to fund ongoing revenue transformation suggests the council is unable to fund change from sustainable revenue sources and is drawing down finite capital assets.
findings.figures: Strategy extended 2026/27 to 2028/29; receipts funding transformation/business change
findings.quote: The proposed strategy for the coming years is more ambitious in this regard than in previous years, recognising the Council's particularly difficult funding position for the next three years

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Essential property maintenance backlog remains unfunded despite capital allocation
findings.detail: The council has allocated £1.455m for property maintenance and prioritised urgent works, but states explicitly that essential and lower-priority works will remain unaddressed. Deferred maintenance risks building deterioration, closure, health/safety risk.
findings.matters: Unmet maintenance backlogs signal deferred cost, future emergency spending, or eventual capital asset impairment or closure.
findings.figures: £1.455m allocated for property maintenance; £200k for revenue-only works
findings.quote: These combined bids will address the most urgent backlog, but essential and lower-priority works will remain.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Aging highways infrastructure requires catch-up investment but capacity has been diminished by inflation
findings.detail: Bracknell's inherited 'new town' infrastructure is now 40–60 years old and many components are failing simultaneously. Recent inflation has cut spending power despite council increasing highways funding. A comprehensive plan is pending.
findings.matters: Deferred highways maintenance becomes expensive crises; unexpectedly rapid deterioration can trigger emergency spending or service disruption.
findings.figures: Infrastructure as old as 60 years; council increased highways funding in 2024/25 and continued support planned to 2027/28
findings.quote: as many components of our highway infrastructure are starting to need intervention at the same time, with some being as old as 60 years. Recent inflation has significantly diminished spending capacity

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Schools no longer receive basic needs grant; capital now entirely council or unfunded
findings.detail: Schools received £1.3m grant in 2025/26 but the council expects no basic needs grant in 2026/27. Schools capital maintenance will be competed against all other council priorities.
findings.matters: Loss of earmarked grants increases pressure on the general fund and may force trade-offs between school condition and other services.
findings.figures: £1.3m received 2025/26, £0m expected 2026/27 for basic needs
findings.quote: Whilst funding of £1.3m was received in 2025/26 the council is not expected to receive any grant in 2026/27 with regards to basic needs grant (primarily used for new school places.)

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Council has sold most surplus property; limited future capital receipt generation expected
findings.detail: The council has divested most of its portfolio of surplus property, leaving little scope to generate capital receipts through further sales. A commercial property review is underway but progress is uncertain.
findings.matters: Without property sales, the council cannot reduce borrowing needs and will remain dependent on CIL, external grants, and debt to fund capital schemes.
findings.figures: Most surplus properties already sold; commercial review underway with uncertain outcome
findings.quote: The council has sold most of its surplus properties over the last few years. As such there is limited scope to fund this or future capital programmes from miscellaneous receipts.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Five-year cash balance depletion has eliminated internal borrowing capacity
findings.detail: Cash reserves have been gradually drawn down over five years to fund prior capital and support the general fund. The council now has no cash available for internal borrowing, forcing all future capital to be financed externally.
findings.matters: Loss of internal borrowing capacity locks the council into external debt markets, increasing vulnerability to interest rate rises and reducing financial autonomy.
findings.figures: Five-year cumulative depletion, no reserves available for internal borrowing
findings.quote: Over the past five years, the council's cash balances have been gradually reduced as they have been used to fund previous capital decisions and support the general fund. These cash reserves are no longer available for internal borrowing purposes.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Capital receipts reserves exhausted: zero balance at March 2025
findings.detail: The council has depleted its balance of usable capital receipts (£0 at 31 March 2025), having applied them all to prior capital investment. This removes the buffer that normally allows affordable internal borrowing and forces external borrowing at market rates.
findings.matters: Lenders care about reserve depletion because it signals limited financial cushion and dependency on external debt at volatile interest rates.
findings.figures: Total usable capital receipts £0 at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Council's total usable capital receipts generated from disposing of assets at 31st March 2025 are zero as all receipts have been applied to fund prior capital investment.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Cabinet Feb 26 Final SMcK
findings.headline: Unfinanced capital gap of £4.051m will require external borrowing
findings.detail: The council projects capital receipts of £4m but requires £8.051m council funding, leaving a shortfall that must be borrowed from PWLB or similar. This adds interest costs and borrowing charges to the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Increased debt burden worsens debt service costs and constrains future financial flexibility, particularly if interest rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: £8.051m council-funded requirement, £4.0m projected receipts, £4.051m unfinanced gap, £0.086m interest cost 2026/27, £0.172m ongoing from 2027/28
findings.quote: leaving an unfinanced request of £4.051m

findings.headline: External borrowing increased since 2023/24 and likely to continue increasing; council has exhausted internal resources for capital financing
findings.detail: The council states: "For many years the Council was able to use internal resources to fund its annual capital programme, with borrowing reserved primarily for one-off large capital investments. However, since 2023/24 these resources became fully utilised, and the Council has increased its level of external borrowing to support capital expenditure. The level of external borrowing is likely to increase annually; however, it should remain substantially below the Capital Financing Requirement over the next 3 years." The 2026/27 capital programme proposes Council funded capital of £8.051m and externally funded of £4.779m. PWLB borrowing rates remain high (five-year rates expected 4.20% by end 2026) despite Bank of England rate cuts, due to "domestic fiscal pressures and global factors."
findings.matters: The council is shifting to structural reliance on external borrowing for capital, not by choice but because internal resources are depleted. This locks in future borrowing costs. With MRP requirements also fixed, the council's revenue is increasingly committed to debt service. If borrowing continues to grow annually and interest rates remain elevated, MRP and interest costs will consume a growing share of controllable budget.
findings.figures: Council capital programme 2026/27: £8.051m council funded + £4.779m externally funded; PWLB five-year rates expected 4.20% by end 2026; estimated additional revenue costs £0.161m in 2026/27 and £0.445m in 2027/28
findings.quote: Since 2023/24 these resources became fully utilised, and the Council has increased its level of external borrowing to support capital expenditure. The level of external borrowing is likely to increase annually

findings.headline: Collection fund council tax deficit of £0.866m in 2025/26, driven by fewer properties added to list than budgeted
findings.detail: The Council Tax element of the collection fund will generate a deficit in the current year (2025/26) primarily because "fewer properties being added to the list during the year than budgeted." The council's share of this one-off deficit is £0.866m, which "increases the budget gap reported in December." This represents a variance between the council's assumption about property growth and actual delivery, suggesting either lower housing completions or slower band registrations than assumed.
findings.matters: Council tax is the most significant sustainable local revenue source, and the council is banking on growing the tax base to offset grant reductions. A shortfall in property growth in 2025/26 suggests the growth assumption may be optimistic. Housing development delays or slower-than-expected migration could undermine future base assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.866m council tax collection fund deficit share in 2025/26
findings.quote: A deficit will be generated on the Council Tax element of the Collection Fund in the current year, primarily due to fewer properties being added to the list during the year than budgeted. The Council's share of this one-off deficit is £0.866m

findings.headline: Pay award settlements higher than budgeted; staffing cost pressures from permanent workforce growth and inability to manage vacancies
findings.detail: The council identifies staffing costs as a key risk area. The 2025/26 pay award "was settled at a higher increase than was budgeted." While spending on agency workers has been reduced, this has created "additional costs of a permanent workforce, due to incremental progression and incentives to promote permanent recruitment." The council is allocating £1.273m to increase devolved staffing budgets to "reduce the required Managed Vacancy Factor by 2% as the current budget level is unsustainable." The council also identifies "Attracting and retaining a suitably qualified, permanent workforce to deliver quality services to residents" as a key strategic risk.
findings.matters: Staffing is the largest cost base for local government and represents structural inflation risk. Public sector pay is subject to national living wage increases and national insurance contributions (explicitly mentioned as a budget risk). The council's inability to maintain the Managed Vacancy Factor at budgeted levels suggests either vacancy control is reaching its limit, or recruitment difficulties are forcing permanent appointments at higher cost. This indicates cost pressures may continue even if recruitment gets tighter.
findings.figures: £1.273m additional allocation to reduce Managed Vacancy Factor by 2%
findings.quote: the 2025/26 pay award was settled at a higher increase than was budgeted and recent success in reducing the level of spending on agency workers has led to additional costs of a permanent workforce, due to incremental progression and incentives to promote permanent recruitment

findings.headline: Rising social care demographic pressures: adult transitions (aging population), children's placements increasing, SEND-related transport costs growing
findings.detail: The council faces "Increasing pressures on front-line services due to changing demographics, increases in needs and associated costs." Specific pressures include: rising cost of supporting looked-after children, increasing support pressures from people living longer, impact of new housing developments, and growth in demand for School Transport particularly for EHCP pupils. A revision in January identified an additional pressure of £0.359m for children's demographic pressures in 2026/27, and projected growth in school transport costs has increased by £0.137m based on 2025/26 pressure and further growth expectations. The council is investing £0.130m to "help reduce the cost of adult social care transitions in future years."
findings.matters: These are demand-led pressures the council cannot refuse and cannot easily control. Aging population and SEND-identified pupils are rising both locally and nationally, so this is not cyclical. Transport and social care are labor-intensive, subject to wage inflation, and compete for finite staffing in a tight labor market. These pressures will likely persist and grow.
findings.figures: £0.359m additional children's social care demographic pressure 2026/27; £0.137m growth in school transport pressure; £0.130m invested to reduce adult social care transition costs
findings.quote: Projected growth in the demand for School Transport and Fleet, based on the pressure in 2025/26 and further growth for 2026/27, has increased. This has been offset by an additional saving relating to the review and re-procurement of Transport Routes

findings.headline: £22.8m Safety Valve reserve locked up; council has written to government asking for release after 2028 but no confirmation
findings.detail: The council maintains a £22.8m earmarked reserve committed to the Safety Valve agreement with DfE. This reserve is unavailable for general fund purposes. The council has written to the Minister for Local Government asking for release of this reserve for other purposes once future DSG deficit funding arrangements are published after the statutory override ends (31 March 2028). However, "There has been no indication how this will be funded or how much support there will be for existing historic deficits." The Executive Director notes "Against a backdrop of the proposed 2026/27 budget that will be reliant on using around £5m of reserves to achieve a balanced position...the importance of addressing the future of Council's £22.8m Safety Valve reserve cannot be overstated."
findings.matters: This is a locked reserve that cannot be deployed for medium-term financial pressures, yet the council is otherwise relying on reserves to bridge deficits. The uncertainty about whether government will absorb or require council coverage of historic SEND deficits creates a contingent liability that could force either service cuts or further reserve depletion from 2028 onwards.
findings.figures: £22.8m Safety Valve earmarked reserve; statutory override end date 31 March 2028; council requires unfettered access to all reserves beyond 2027/28
findings.quote: The Autumn Budget 2025 confirmed that the future costs of SEND will be funded by Central Government after the Statutory Override ends. While it is positive the Government has committed to absorbing the costs of SEND spending from 2028/29 there has been no indication how this will be funded or how much support there will be for existing historic deficits which will continue to grow until March 2028.

findings.headline: High Needs Block dedicated schools grant in deficit: £9.839m overspend 2025/26, forecast £8.327m for 2026/27, with rising SEND pupil numbers
findings.detail: The council is party to a Department for Education Safety Valve agreement after the High Needs Block (HNB) schools budget fell into deficit. Current overspend stands at £9.839m for 2025/26 with forecast overspend of £8.327m in 2026/27 before any council investment. The deficit is driven by underfunding of current commitments plus "further increases in costs expected as the numbers of pupils requiring support and the complexity of need increase as well as general inflationary pressures." EHCP numbers are rising both locally and nationally. Although a statutory override allows DSG deficit to be carried forward as a "negative reserve" until 31 March 2028, the Government has only notionally committed to funding SEND from 2028/29 with no clarity on mechanics or historic deficit coverage.
findings.matters: This represents a material unfunded contingent liability. The council cannot reduce this spending without reducing legal support for children with identified SEND needs. The statutory override ends 2028, creating a cliff-edge refinancing requirement that government has not yet guaranteed to fund. This is the most significant risk to the council's medium-term budget.
findings.figures: £9.839m HNB overspend 2025/26; £8.327m forecast overspend 2026/27; £22.8m Safety Valve earmarked reserve; statutory override ends 31 March 2028
findings.quote: the amount of income received is insufficient to fund the forecast costs which for 2025/26 amounted to an overspend for the year and at the latest monitoring this now stands at £9.839m. This primarily arises from underfunding of current commitments with further increases in costs expected as the numbers of pupils requiring support and the complexity of need increase

findings.headline: Council using approximately £10m of one-off resources to balance budget; strategy explicitly described as "not sustainable"
findings.detail: To achieve a balanced 2026/27 budget, the council will deploy around £10m of one-off resources comprising: ~£5m from reserves, use of capital receipts flexibility (£1.987m), and collection fund surpluses (£1.627m business rates surplus offset partly by £0.866m council tax deficit). The Executive Director explicitly states "this is not a sustainable financial strategy" and notes that "future spending pressures of around £10m per year will not be covered by funding increases." The council is entering a structural deficit that requires fundamental service redesign.
findings.matters: A lender assessing medium-term repayment capacity must understand this is temporary crisis management, not sustainable finance. The council acknowledges it cannot continue this approach and is dependent on either transformational cost reduction or service model changes that may not materialise quickly enough.
findings.figures: ~£10m one-off resources for 2026/27; ~£5m from reserves; £1.987m capital receipts; £1.627m business rates collection fund surplus; £0.866m council tax deficit
findings.quote: We have no realistic option in the 2026/27 but to draw significantly on our reserves and use capital receipts flexibly to support the revenue budget. We understand that these resources are finite and can only be spent once.

findings.headline: Business rates reset delivers £1.964m income hit; council was highest beneficiary under old system and faces major loss
findings.detail: For the first time since 2013, the Business Rates Retention System has been reset to reflect updated needs assessments. Bracknell Forest was proportionately one of the highest beneficiaries of the old system; the reset reallocates funding to more deprived areas. The NNDR1 return (which sets the budget for business rates) now indicates income equal only to the baseline funding level with no growth forecast, resulting in £1.964m less income than assumed in December draft. Partial compensation of £0.859m comes through transitional protection funding.
findings.matters: The reset is structural, not temporary. The council lost significant retained business rates growth income overnight, replaced only by transitional protection that phases out by 2028/29. This demonstrates how funding architecture changes can substantially reduce council income independent of economic conditions.
findings.figures: £1.964m income shortfall; £0.859m transitional protection in 2026/27; no business rates growth forecast for 2026/27
findings.quote: This is £1.964m less income than had been assumed in the draft budget proposals and primarily relates to the complexities of the treatment of section 31 grant under the system changes.

findings.headline: Worst funding settlement of any unitary authority: £223k increase over three years cannot cover £10m annual inflation and demand pressures
findings.detail: Bracknell Forest faces the lowest core spending power increase of any unitary authority over 2026/27 to 2028/29, with a total increase of just £223,000 (0.16% of £135m core spending power). This comprises an £18m reduction in grant and business rates income offset by assumption of 4.99% council tax increases and growing tax base. Annual spending pressures typically amount to £10m, which the settlement cannot cover. The Executive Director states this is "wholly inadequate."
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the structural deficit the council faces is not cyclical; it reflects a permanent shift in the funding system that will not improve without spending cuts or tax rises that may face political resistance.
findings.figures: £223,000 total increase over three years; £18m reduction in grant and business rates by 2028/29; £10m annual spending pressures; 0.16% increase on £135m budget
findings.quote: A total increase in spending power of £223,000 over the next three years clearly does not recognise the spending pressures that this Council faces.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs have spiked to 55 basis points above base rate, the widest spread in five years, with officers warning of potential Q4 budget pressure
findings.detail: Local authority inter-lending markets are severely constrained, with demand outstripping supply. Three-month borrowing rates are trading above 4.25%, creating a 55 basis point premium over base rate—one of the widest spreads in five years and worse than last year. The Council has attempted to secure sufficient short-term borrowing to manage liquidity risk, but officers explicitly warn that working capital requirements in the final quarter may bring further budget pressure.
findings.matters: Elevated short-term borrowing costs directly inflate the Council's interest bill and create cash flow strain. The officers' explicit warning of Q4 budget pressure indicates this is not routine commentary but a live financial risk.
findings.figures: 3-month borrowing at over 4.25%; 55 basis point premium over base rate; spread described as one of the widest in last 5 years
findings.quote: Current 3-month offers between local authorities are trading at over 4.25% - a premium of 55 basis points over the base rate and reflecting one of the widest spreads between borrowing and investment rates in the last 5 years and presenting even more challenging conditions than last year. However, with such liquidity shortage working capital requirements may bring further budget pressure in the last quarter.

findings.headline: Bracknell Forest has exhausted internal resources and shifted to external borrowing to fund capital, with further annual increases expected
findings.detail: The Council historically funded its capital programme from internal resources, but these have been fully depleted since 2023/24. External borrowing has increased to support capital schemes and is expected to grow annually going forward. The Council holds £55m in short-term market loans and £60m in PWLB loans as at 30 November 2025, with average rates ranging from 2.14% to 4.80% across the portfolio.
findings.matters: The depletion of internal reserves and reliance on external markets for capital funding signals a structural shift in the Council's financial position. This has implications for borrowing capacity and financial sustainability that lenders monitor closely.
findings.figures: £55m short-term market loans (rates 4.15%–4.80%); £60m PWLB loans (rates 2.14%–2.60%); shift from internal funding began in 2023/24
findings.quote: However, since 2023/24 these resources were fully utilised, and the Council has increased its level of external borrowing to support past and current capital schemes. The level of external borrowing is likely to increase annually, however should remain substantially below the Capital Financing Requirement (as set out in the TMSS) over the next 3-years

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £24.65m being funded through Safety Valve arrangement but consuming significant reserves
findings.detail: The Council carries a DSG deficit of £24.65m as at 31 March 2025. While Safety Valve funding of £16m and earmarked reserves of £22.8m are in place, the deficit reflects structural pressures in education and SEND. Similar challenges were identified in prior year audit.
findings.matters: A large DSG deficit signals ongoing cost pressures in a key service area and ties up material reserves that could otherwise support general fund flexibility or borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: DSG deficit: £24,650k; Safety Valve funding: £16m; earmarked reserves: £22.8m
findings.quote: Like many Authorities, the Council is carrying a deficit in relation to its Dedicated Schools Grant. As at 31 March 2025 the deficit was £24,650k. The Safety Valve arrangements that the Council is entering in to include £16m of funding to support the clearance of this deficit and an additional £22.8m of earmarked reserves have been set aside.

findings.headline: Uncorrected material audit difference of £7.589m: donated asset recorded in wrong financial year despite quantitative materiality
findings.detail: The Council recorded receipt of Bucklers Park Community Hub in 2024/25, but it was actually received in 2023/24. The finance team was unaware at the time. While the auditors acknowledge the £7.589m error is 'quantitatively material', they have not insisted on correction, citing unspecified qualitative factors.
findings.matters: An uncorrected material error that auditors declined to push for suggests either weak control over asset receipt or unusual audit judgment. The decision not to enforce correction despite materiality indicates possible tensions over what constitutes true materiality.
findings.figures: £7,589m; affects capital grants and Property Plant & Equipment balances
findings.quote: The Council has recorded the receipt of a donated asset (Bucklers Park Community Hub) during the year ending 31 March 2025. We identified that the asset was actually received in the year ending 31 March 2024 but that the finance team had not been made aware of this at the time.

findings.headline: Investment property portfolio overstated by £11.48m due to overly optimistic valuation assumptions; professional disagreement with external valuers
findings.detail: KPMG identified overly optimistic assumptions in market rents and yield rates used by valuers Wilkes Head & Eve, plus discrepancies in floor areas. The auditors have proposed a £11.48m corrected adjustment to reduce the investment property valuation, representing 8.6% of the £134m portfolio. The matter remains in professional disagreement and is still being discussed with management.
findings.matters: A material overstatement of assets suggests control weaknesses in valuation oversight and indicates the true asset base may be lower, affecting collateral value and financial stability.
findings.figures: Overstatement: £11,480k; total investment property portfolio: £134m; comparable floor areas used varied from supporting evidence
findings.quote: Our sample testing identified overly optimistic assumptions in relation to both market rents and yield rates arising from the fact that the comparable evidence used by Wilkes Head & Eve was not directly comparable to the assets under valuation. In addition, we identified one instance where the floor areas used in the valuation varied from supporting evidence.

findings.headline: Auditors issuing disclaimer of opinion due to inability to audit the split between usable and unusable reserves before statutory deadline
findings.detail: KPMG cannot obtain sufficient audit evidence over the reserves split and prior year comparative figures by the 27 February 2026 statutory backstop deadline. The auditors consider this pervasiveness to be material to the Council's entire financial position. The audit is incomplete and the disclaimer will be issued despite rebuilding assurance work.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means financial statements cannot be relied upon. For lenders, the inability to verify reserves—the core indicator of financial stability and borrowing capacity—is disqualifying information.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline: 27 February 2026; inability to audit reserves split and 2023/24 comparatives
findings.quote: Given our work to rebuild assurance is not complete and due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Council's financial position as at 31 March 2025.

news_drafts.headline: Nine schemes carried forward from 2024/25 with zero 2025/26 expenditure; requesting carry-forward again into 2026/27
news_drafts.lead: Multi-year non-spend suggests projects may not be delivery-ready; capital tied up without clear delivery route; pattern indicates project preparation or approvals issues
news_drafts.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1

news_drafts.headline: Council redirected capital receipt to revenue support ('flexible use') due to 'significant pressure on revenue budget' from government funding settlement
news_drafts.lead: Revenue-side stress forcing capital receipts to be used for revenue support rather than capital financing; signals structural revenue deficit; reduces capital financing flexibility
news_drafts.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1

news_drafts.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £20.7m year-on-year to £239.6m; council 'gradually moving away from ability to internally fund capital investment'
news_drafts.lead: Rapid rise in CFR signals deteriorating financial position and increasing reliance on borrowing; reduces financial headroom and increases exposure to interest rate risk; trend unsustainable if capital underdelivery persists
news_drafts.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Report Outturn 25-26 FINAL v2.1
